The Galatea paradoxa clam, a common inhabitant of sandy intertidal zones in West African estuaries, attains a maximum recorded shell length of 11.4 centimeters [Li = 11.4 centimeters], a size that reflects the species' position as one of the larger members of the Donax genus. This ultimate total length is reached only after several years of growth, during which the individuals exhibit the typical wedge-shaped morphology of surf clams adapted to high-energy environments. Field surveys conducted across the species' range have consistently documented adult specimens approaching this asymptotic size, though local conditions such as sediment grain size and food availability can produce considerable variation in the maximum shell dimension observed within a given population.

Sexual maturation in this species is initiated once individuals reach a shell length of 3.6 centimeters [Lp = 3.6 centimeters], a relatively modest size that represents approximately one-third of the ultimate length. This onset of puberty is closely tied to the attainment of a critical body mass, enabling the allocation of resources toward gametogenesis for the first time. Histological examination of gonad tissue from clams collected in the Volta River estuary has confirmed that active spermatogenesis and oogenesis are consistently present in specimens exceeding this length threshold, whereas smaller individuals show no evidence of reproductive tissue development.

At a constant water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the embryonic development of Galatea paradoxa proceeds rapidly, with newly formed zygotes completing the veliger larval stage and hatching from the egg capsule in just 2 days [ab = 2 days]. The resulting yolk-sac larva weighs a mere 0.000004 grams [Wwb = 0.000004 grams] at the moment of hatching, reflecting the tiny egg diameter of approximately 200 micrometers from which it emerges. This brief and energetically efficient incubation period is characteristic of many warm-water bivalves and allows for multiple spawning events within a single reproductive season when thermal conditions remain favorable.

Under the same stable thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the reproductive output of this clam is remarkably high for a bivalve of its size. Mature females release approximately 2740 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2740 eggs per spawning event] during peak spawning, with spawning occurring roughly once per 10 days [F_R_i = roughly once per 10 days]. This combination of fecundity per event and spawning frequency, when integrated over the course of a breeding season, represents a substantial investment in gamete production that is typical of opportunistic r-selected species inhabiting unpredictable coastal environments.

The maximum recorded lifespan for Galatea paradoxa in the wild is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] under the prevailing thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a duration that places it among the longer-lived members of the Donacidae family. A gravid adult nearing the end of its life, with a shell length of 9.74 centimeters, can possess a tissue wet weight of 344.8 grams [Wwi = 344.8 grams], representing the substantial somatic biomass accumulated over a decade or more of filter feeding. This longevity, combined with the capacity for sustained high reproductive output, allows the species to maintain stable populations despite the intense predation pressure exerted by shorebirds and demersal fish throughout its estuarine habitat.
